w: Known in Italian as the Teatro Antico di Taormina, this ancient Greek theatre was cut into the hillside above the town in the third century BC. It survives today as one of Taormina's oldest structures, a stone amphitheatre that has outlasted most of what Hellenistic Sicily built around it.
s: Greek theatre carved into the hillside, 3rd c. BC
_facts: Italian name: Teatro antico di Taormina

w: Ancient Naxos was a Greek city of Magna Graecia on Sicily's east coast, its ruins lying beneath and beside modern Giardini Naxos, just along the shore from Taormina. Much of the site was never built over, and recent-decades excavations have opened its remains to visitors, alongside an on-site museum of finds.
s: Magna Graecia ruins beneath Giardini Naxos
_facts: Ancient Greek city of Magna Graecia
Remains open to public with on-site museum

w: Known as the Pearl of the Ionian Sea, this small island sits in a bay off Taormina, linked to the beach by a narrow path. Once owned by Florence Trevelyan, it was bought by the Region of Sicily in 1990 and is now a WWF-run nature reserve ringed by sea grottoes, its beach popular with sunbathers.
s: Private island turned nature reserve off Taormina
_facts: Called the Pearl of the Ionian Sea
Bought by the Region of Sicily in 1990, now a WWF reserve
Surrounded by sea grottoes; linked to shore by a narrow path

w: Named after the Corvaja family, who owned it from 1538 to 1945, this crenellated Catalan Gothic palace in Taormina was built mainly at the end of the 14th century around a central courtyard. Its walls carry relief carvings of the Creation, and a 13th-century Arab tower survives inside; today it hosts exhibitions.
s: Medieval palace with an Arab tower and Creation reliefs
_facts: Built mainly at the end of the 14th century
Catalan Gothic style, crenellated, courtyard reliefs of the Creation
Incorporates a 13th-century Arab tower; now an exhibition space
